endorsements.quote: In addition to technical oversight, robust governance models must be established to define accountability for clinical outcomes.

To solve these issues, autonomous smart devices intended for clinical use should obtain appropriate regulatory approval, such as FDA or CE certification, with regulatory standards tailored to their classification98,99.
Furthermore, healthcare professionals must remain vigilant against automation bias and be prepared to critically evaluate and override AI-generated outputs when necessary.
Furthermore, developers should incorporate explainability and human-in-the-loop mechanisms into EAI systems to enhance transparency, reliability and trust in clinical environments.

unlisted_practices: Adopt a tiered consent framework for EAI systems that distinguishes physiologic data requiring strict authorization from environmental interaction metadata that can be broadly authorized.
Adopt a dynamic consent process allowing patients to modify or withdraw consent at any time.
Adopt bias mitigation strategies and develop data governance frameworks emphasizing diversity and transparency.
Develop standardized, multidimensional evaluation frameworks for embodied AI that include interactive scenarios beyond static data and traditional metrics.
Expand the medical knowledge base within embodied AI to ensure its accuracy, safety, and reliability in ophthalmic practice.
Computer scientists and healthcare professionals should collaborate to refine autonomy classification criteria for embodied AI.

screen.reason: This is a perspective article exploring the concepts, potential, challenges, and future directions of embodied AI in ophthalmology rather than an empirical study.
